title: Cross products explained: 2D area intuition, 3D vector result, and a determinant-based construction
summary: This two-part module opener surveys the standard 2D cross product intuition as the signed area of the parallelogram spanned by two vectors, emphasizing how orientation (order of V and W) determines the sign and how a determinant computes that area via the matrix with V and W as columns. The video then shifts to the true 3D cross product, describing it as a vector whose length equals the parallelogram area and whose direction is perpendicular to the plane, determined by the right-hand rule. A mnemonic determinant procedure in 3D is introduced: form a matrix with I, J, K in the first column and the coordinates of V and W in the other columns, then take its determinant to obtain the cross product vector. The host notes deeper geometric ideas (duality) in a follow-up video and clarifies the distinction between the 2D signed-area intuition and the full 3D cross product.

sections.description: The video introduces the 2D cross product by visualizing the parallelogram spanned by V and W. The cross product in 2D is treated as the signed area of that parallelogram, with sign determined by orientation (positive when V is on the right of W). The basis vectors I_hat and J_hat anchor the orientation convention, and placing V and W as the columns of a matrix makes the determinant equal to this signed area (the area factor under the linear transformation sending I_hat, J_hat to V, W).

sections.title: Right-hand rule and 3D cross product intuition
concepts: Cross product as a vector (not a scalar) in 3D
Example with perpendicular vectors yielding a 4-unit cross product
sections.description: The discussion transitions from the 2D scalar cross product to the true 3D cross product, describing it as a vector whose length equals the parallelogram area and whose direction is perpendicular to the plane, determined by the right-hand rule. An illustrative example uses perpendicular vectors to show the cross product magnitude and direction (e.g., a square parallelogram with area 4 pointing along the appropriate axis).

sections.description: A mnemonic, determinant-based procedure is presented for computing the 3D cross product by forming a matrix with I_hat, J_hat, and K_hat in the first column and the coordinates of V and W in the other two columns. The determinant produces the cross product vector. The instructor notes that this is a notational device with a meaningful geometric interpretation and hints at deeper duality ideas that will be covered in a follow-up video.
